title: Pilot study of a smart in tracheal tube designed to monitor breathing and body functions (iTraXS 1)
official: Physiological sensing capabilities of a novel IntraTRAcheal multipleXed Sensing tube: a pilot clinical trial with feasibility assessment (iTraXS 1)
summary:
Background and study aims  
When people have surgery under general anaesthetic, a breathing tube is used to help them breathe safely. The position of this tube and the pressure of its cuff must be correct to avoid problems such as low oxygen levels, airway injury, or fluid leaking into the lungs. At the moment, breathing tubes do not give direct information about what is happening inside the airway, so doctors must rely on external monitors, which can sometimes be unreliable.

The iTraXS tube is a new breathing tube that contains very small fibre optic sensors. These sensors can measure oxygen levels and blood flow inside the airway and can help check whether the tube has been correctly placed in the windpipe. This study is the first to test the iTraXS tube in real patients during planned surgery. The aim is to find out whether the sensors work well, whether they can help confirm tube position, whether staff can use the device easily, and whether enough patients can be recruited for a future larger study.

Who can participate?  
Up to 40 adults aged 18 to 70 years who are having planned surgery that already requires a breathing tube and an arterial line can take part. People with certain medical conditions, such as difficult airways, severe reflux, or pregnancy, cannot join the study for safety reasons.

What does the study involve?
Participants will receive their usual NHS care. The only differences are:
• The standard breathing tube will be replaced with the new iTraXS tube  
• A second iTraXS tube will be gently placed in the food pipe (oesophagus) for a short time to take comparison readings  
• A few extra blood samples will be taken from the arterial line, which is already in place, so no extra needles are needed

The sensors will collect information during the operation. All data will be stored securely and anonymously. Participants will be reviewed the day after surgery, and their involvement then ends.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?  
There is no direct medical benefit to participants. However, the results could help improve the safety of breathing tubes and airway monitoring for people having surgery in the future.

The risks are similar to those of standard breathing tubes. These include a sore throat or hoarse voice, and a very small risk of airway irritation or injury. Extra blood samples carry minimal risk as they are taken from a line that is already in place. If the iTraXS tube cannot be placed easily, the anaesthetist will stop and use a standard tube instead. Usual NHS care always comes first.

Where is the study run from?  
The study is run from Queens Medical Centre at Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?  
The study is expected to begin on 1 May 2026 and will run for 12 months.

Who is funding the study?  
The study is funded by the Medical Research Council (UK) MR/Y008642/1.

Who is the main contact?  
The Chief Investigator is Dr David Hewson, david.hewson@nottingham.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age 18 - 70 years
2. Undergoing elective surgery with planned tracheal intubation and arterial catheterisation as part of routine NHS clinical care
3. Able to provide informed written consent
Exclusion criteria:
1. Known or predicted difficult facemask ventilation or tracheal intubation
2. Previous and planned laryngeal, tracheal or oesophageal surgery
3. History of dysphagia or achalasia  
4. History of uncontrolled gastro-oesophageal reflux or known hiatus hernia 
5. History of pharyngeal pouch 
6. Risk of pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents necessitating awake or rapid sequence tracheal intubation 
7. Pregnancy
